comments.author: @DemMedHornene
comments.text:
As a Dane living in Japan with my Japanese wife, I think the main issues besides the obvious work culture stuff (which is improving, but very slowly), is the family traditions. It is a *massive* source of family friction when you get married, and families do not come together that often, with it being more common that the wife joins the husband's family, but then the new year's tradition is still to visit your own family. I think this remains one of the biggest barriers, because, when coupled with work stress, incomes not matching inflation, education being absurdly expensive, and so on, rigid family structures makes even the simple act of marriage a major hassle. And frankly, as a man, the Japanese laws about custody are extremely off-putting, since, hypothetically, if I have a kid with my wife, she could divorce and take the child and I would have zero legal recourse to see my child.

It's easy to point to one or two things as being the causes, but I think that, quite frankly, Japan has the perfect storm of elements that make the idea of having children extremely off-putting to most people. I don't even think immigration really fixes the issue either, because after a few generations, their childbirths will fall to match everyone else's, so it's just kicking the can down the road, rather than finding a sustainable solution.

All that being said, at least in Tokyo, I have been seeing a lot more babies this last year from Japanese families, buuut, there are still more baby strollers used for dogs than children, and it's generally more common to see more children in the lower-income wards ^-^
